lines: We came back with all our pieces where they belong. Good enough for my ledger.
The first thread of smoke above home nearly took my legs out from under me.
We reached the gate with enough food left for one last shared meal.
Seeing the smokehouse roof again made my knees go weak.
You brought enough food that hunger never made our choices for us.
I noticed every time you slowed down without making a fuss about it.
The first locked door on the way home felt like a promise.
We slept beside the road, but you kept the fire low and the watch steady.
I had saved one good ration for trouble. We ate it when the village came into view.
You found clean water before my own flask ran dry.
Nothing followed us through the gate except dust and relief.
I checked the stores before bed, then slept until the next afternoon.
Home smelled of oak smoke, animals, and supper. I nearly cried.
You never treated my work bag like useless weight.
We avoided a bad stretch of road because you listened when I objected.
The village had kept my smoker cold. Lighting it again felt like returning.
I came home hungry instead of wounded. That is a successful journey.
You shared the last crust without waiting for me to ask.
I trust your directions now, though I still pack for getting lost.
The trip was hard. Being left alone would have been harder.
I know a shallow cut from a deep mistake. That trip had a little of both.
I came home bleeding through a cloth that should have been wrapping supper.
If we take that road again, the bandages go above the food in my pack.
The cut looked small until every step pulled it open.
You used the last clean food cloth for my bandage without hesitation.
I hated slowing us down more than I hated the pain.
We had to leave supplies behind so I could keep walking.
You found a branch for me to lean on before I admitted I needed it.
The smell of blood made me think of work, which was no comfort at all.
I remember you checking the bandage whenever we stopped for water.
A dry piece of bread became a full meal once I was too tired to argue.
The village bell sounded impossibly far away that evening.
You carried my cleaver after my hand stopped closing properly.
I still feel that wound when I lift a heavy barrel.
The healer said another night outside would have gone badly.
I learned not to call an injury shallow before the bleeding stops.
You kept your voice calm while mine grew short and ugly.
I owe you an apology for every time I claimed I could walk faster.
The first bowl of broth back home stayed down. That was the turning point.
Next time I pack bandages beside the food instead of under it.
I expect sharp things at work. I did not expect one from the person I followed.
I followed you with a full pack and honest trust. Only the pack came home intact.
I expect danger from the road, not from the person eating my provisions.
You knew the road was unsafe and let me carry on as if it were not.
I packed food for a journey, not for being used as bait.
The danger was honest. You were not.
I remember reaching for my cleaver because I no longer trusted the person beside me.
You chose the risk for both of us and explained it only afterward.
Getting me home does not cancel the moment you left me exposed.
I gave you my trust as plainly as I would hand over a clean tool.
The wound closed faster than my suspicion did.
I still check every route you suggest against someone else's word.
You ate from the supplies I packed while hiding the truth from me.
Do not call it protection when I was never allowed to decide.
I came back to my smokehouse and changed the lock that same night.
If you want forgiveness, tell me what you were thinking without trimming it pretty.
I survived because I stopped following your instructions.
The village welcomed us both. Only one of us deserved the welcome.
Time has cooled my anger enough to speak, not enough to trust.
Next time I decide which dangers are mine.
I prefer a steady block beneath me, but the boat got us back without carving a new problem.
The boat carried us home, though I spent the crossing expecting it to change its mind.
<aqua><wavy>Water</wavy></aqua> got us back. A dry smokehouse floor finished the rescue.
I packed for a road and learned too late that the road floated.
The provisions stayed dry because you tied the sacks better than I did.
We ate cold food while the waves made a cooking fire ridiculous.
I watched the shore shrink until even the village smoke disappeared.
The boat leaked slowly enough to keep me worried the entire way.
You rowed while I bailed, which was the fairest arrangement available.
Salt water found every cut on my hands.
I saved the best ration for land and nearly ate it three times.
The sound of water against the hull followed me into my first night home.
You spotted the landing while I was still arguing with a cloud.
I stepped into shore mud and thanked it for being solid.
Every distant tree looked like our village until we drew closer.
I would bring less glass and more rope on another crossing.
The current took us wide, but you never let the food bag go overboard.
We arrived soaked enough to drip across the smokehouse floor.
A hot supper stopped the ground from swaying under me.
I would take that boat again, though I would inspect every plank first.
